[Management API](admin-api.html)

What happened here, in order — history rather than state, and read-only. It carries no credential of any kind and has no clear operation: an erase control on an administrative surface would make an audit log unable to answer the one question it exists for.

Every answer is checked against the model shown here before it is sent, and no answer carries a member its model does not list. A member shown as *any JSON* is one whose shape belongs to somebody else, and says whose. `.{key}` is a key that is data, and `[]` an element of a list.

| `ok` | boolean |  |  |
| `status` | integer |  |  |
| `why` | string |  |  |

## GET /admin-api/audit

`getAudit`

**What happened here, in order, filtered and paged**

Every authentication, session, LDAP directory operation, console interaction, management API call and protocol endpoint call, newest first.

This is HISTORY where the rest of this API is STATE. /admin-api/metrics can say the directory holds eleven entries; only this can say a twelfth was created at 14:02 and deleted at 14:03 by somebody bound as `uid=carol`, over LDAPS.

**NO CREDENTIAL IS EVER IN A ROW.** Not a password, not a bearer token, not an assertion, and no request or response body. A modify names the attributes it changed and never their values, because a modify is where a `userPassword` gets set; a compare says whether it matched and not what was tried; an authorization code in a query string is replaced with `(redacted)`.

**One act usually produces several events.** A sign-in writes three — the HTTP call, the credential being accepted, and the session that came out of it. They are three facts at three layers, and a Kerberos AS-REQ authenticates somebody and starts no session at all.

RESUME BY `at`, not by page. Every event has a `seq` that is unique across every process of the service and never reused, including across a drop and a restart, and that rises within each process (#465). It is NOT one order across processes — request workers and cluster nodes each number from blocks of their own — so read what is new by `at`, with `seq` (and `origin`) as the tie-break and as the event's name.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/audit` on the admin console.

Scope: `admin:read`.

## GET /admin-api/audit/integrity

`getAuditIntegrity`

**Check the held audit rows against their checksums**

Each row carries a keyed checksum whose key is not in the database, and the checksum of the row its process wrote before it. `altered` lists the seq of any row that no longer matches. `missing` lists each place a row is gone from between two held rows of one process. `head` says whether this process's newest row is still there: `intact`; `truncated` when its newest rows were removed; `altered` when the record of which row is newest was changed; `none` when it has written no signed row. The oldest rows leave by design at `audit.maxEvents`. `unsigned` counts rows written with no key-encryption key in the process.

Scope: `admin:read`.

**Parameters**

| Name | In | Type | Required | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DPoP` | header | string |  | RFC 9449: the proof of possession for a DPoP-bound access token, as `Authorization: DPoP <token>` requires. |
| `cell` | query | string |  | The cell to answer this request, where this service runs as several. Ignored in a service that runs as one. |

**200**: The result.

| Member | Type | Required | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `altered` | list | yes |  |
| `altered[]` | integer |  |  |
| `checked` | integer | yes |  |
| `head` | one of `intact`, `truncated`, `altered`, `none` | yes |  |
| `missing` | list | yes |  |
| `missing[].after` | integer | yes |  |
| `missing[].before` | integer | yes |  |
| `missing[].origin` | string | yes |  |
| `unsigned` | integer | yes |  |

## GET /admin-api/error-codes

`getErrorCodes`

**Every failure condition this service can produce, and how often each is on the held audit log**

The central table of error codes, `STS-<SUBSYSTEM>-<NNNN>`, filtered and paged: each code with the subsystem it belongs to, what failed, and what the CLIENT is told in its protocol's own vocabulary (`spec`).

**A CODE IS NEVER SENT TO A CLIENT.** It is recorded on the audit row (`errorCode` on GET /admin-api/audit, filterable there with `?code=`) and at the front of the service log line; every protocol response is exactly what it was.

`seen` counts the rows the audit log holds IN THIS REALM right now, so it falls as the log's cap discards the oldest, and it is zero for a failure recorded only as a log line — a startup refusal, or anything the remote PEP container records. `unregisteredSeen` lists codes found on held rows that the table does not hold, each a failure site whose code was never registered.

The same table is published as docs/error-codes.md, generated from common/error_codes.js.

**Mirrors** `GET /admin/error-codes` on the admin console.

Scope: `admin:read`.

**Parameters**

| Name | In | Type | Required | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `subsystem` | query | string |  | One subsystem id — `OAUTH`, `LDAP`, `XPEP` — as `subsystems[].id` lists them. Case-insensitive. |
| `q` | query | string |  | Substring of the code, the summary or what the client sees, case-insensitive — a code pasted out of a log line, or a protocol error name such as `invalid_grant`. |
| `seen` | query | string |  | `1` for only the codes on at least one held audit row. |
| `page` | query | integer |  | Which page of the match to return. CLAMPED rather than refused: a page past the end returns the last one, and the reply says which page it actually is. |
| `per` | query | integer |  | Rows per page. Defaults to 50 and is capped at 300. On a drill-down it is SHARED by every list in the reply, which each carry a page number of their own. |
| `DPoP` | header | string |  | RFC 9449: the proof of possession for a DPoP-bound access token, as `Authorization: DPoP <token>` requires. |
| `cell` | query | string |  | The cell to answer this request, where this service runs as several. Ignored in a service that runs as one. |

**200**: The matching codes, the subsystems with their counts, and the paging that found them.
